segments.line: That night, you don't sleep. You don't want to waste a single hour.
Ellie climbs into your bed, the way you used to climb into hers.
Except that never happened. It just feels like it did now.
'Are you going away? ' she asks. You tell her the truth.
If you stay, you get one more week. Every day smaller. Every night forgetting a little more. And then nobody knows.
If you go, you might get years. But you don't see her. Not her birthday. Not her first day at her new school. Maybe not ever.
Ellie thinks about it for a long time, which for an eight- year- old is about nine seconds.
'Go, ' she says. 'If you go, then when I'm big, you'll still be my brother. ' She
gives you her stuffed rabbit, the one she's had since she was a baby. 'He
sleeps all day, ' she says. 'Like babies. ' She's right.
Newborns sleep fourteen to seventeen hours a day. That's real.
She just doesn't want you to sleep alone. At
five to midnight, a black car waits outside with its headlights off. You
hug your mom. You hug
Mo, who's pretending not to cry and is really bad at it. And
Ellie stands at the window, waving, until the car turns the corner. In
the back seat, you hold the rabbit and watch your street slide by. Your
house. The roof where you made the list. Mo's bike, lying on the lawn.
Midnight. You
feel the shift.
Six years old.
